title: Three Red Panda Cubs Are the Zoo's Big Celebration
summary:
Happy International Red Panda Day! The Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington, D.C., has three fluffy reasons to celebrate this year.

Three red panda cubs were born this summer at the zoo's conservation campus in Front Royal, Virginia. On May 29, a 3-year-old mom named Sequoia and a 12-year-old dad named Mow Mow welcomed twins — one female and one male. On June 11, another 3-year-old mom named Keahi gave birth to a single female cub. Her dad is a 7-year-old named Rocket.

"The new cubs are ensuring the population overall," said Jessica Kordell, assistant curator of carnivores. "We can't conserve the species and continue to breed them if we don't have the animals."

The cubs have spent the summer tucked in nest boxes with their parents, drinking milk and sleeping. All three are doing well. Staff have started putting bamboo in their boxes, but the cubs haven't tried eating it yet.

The singleton is feisty and "huff-quacks" at people. The twins are quieter and shy, and they love to cuddle with each other.

Red pandas are endangered. Less than 10,000 remain in the wild. They live in treetops in Nepal, India, Bhutan, Myanmar, and China. They eat bamboo — a lot of it. They can digest only about 24 percent, so they must eat 20 to 30 percent of their body weight every day. That's like a 60-pound kid eating 12 to 18 pounds of food daily!

Their red fur helps them blend in with lichen that grows on trees. Their black bellies fade into shadows.

Visitors to the zoo's main campus in D.C. can see an adult red panda named Asa on the Asia Trail. The cubs stay at the closed Front Royal facility for now.
why_it_matters: Endangered animals could be gone by the time you grow up, so zoos and kids who care about wildlife both play a part in keeping species like red pandas alive.

background_read: The Smithsonian's National Zoo (a famous zoo in Washington, D.C., run by the Smithsonian, a big American science and museum group) has looked after red pandas for many years, both at its public zoo and at a quieter campus where animals can breed.
In the wild, red pandas live in the mountain forests of the Himalayas, across Nepal, India, Bhutan, Myanmar and China, and cutting down those forests is the main reason their numbers keep falling.
International Red Panda Day is celebrated once a year, when zoos and animal fans around the world try to raise money and attention to help protect these animals.
Article_Structure: WHO: Three red panda cubs, their parents Sequoia, Mow Mow, Keahi and Rocket, and zoo staff including assistant curator Jessica Kordell.
WHAT: The cubs were born this summer — twins to Sequoia and Mow Mow, and a single cub to Keahi — and all three are healthy and growing in their nest boxes.
WHERE: The Smithsonian's National Zoo's conservation campus in Front Royal, Virginia, while an adult red panda named Asa can be seen at the main zoo in Washington, D.C.
WHY: Because red pandas are endangered, with fewer than 10,000 left in the wild, every new cub helps keep the species going for the future.

perspectives.description: They see three healthy cubs as proof that breeding programs work and that zoos can help save a species that is struggling in the wild.
Some people think wild animals should live free in forests, not in nest boxes, and that the real answer is protecting the places red pandas come from.
Three cubs are nice news, but with fewer than 10,000 red pandas left in the wild, zoo births are only a small piece of a much bigger problem.
